title: Conjecture 1.1 (The Edge-statistics Conjecture)
statement_text: For every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $k_0 = k_0(\varepsilon)$ such that for all integers $k > k_0$ and $0 < \ell < \binom{k}{2}$ we have $\mathrm{ind}(k, \ell) \leq 1/e + \varepsilon$.
context_text: For a graph $G$ on $n$ vertices and $0\le\ell\le\binom k2$, let $I(n,k,\ell)$ be the maximum, over graphs $G$ on $n$ vertices, of the probability that a uniformly random $k$-subset of $V(G)$ spans exactly $\ell$ edges; this is non-increasing in $n$, and the edge-inducibility is $\mathrm{ind}(k,\ell)=\lim_{n\to\infty}I(n,k,\ell)$. It equals $1$ for $\ell\in\{0,\binom k2\}$ (empty or complete graphs) and satisfies $\mathrm{ind}(k,\ell)=\mathrm{ind}(k,\binom k2-\ell)$. For a graph $H$, the inducibility $\mathrm{ind}(H)$ (Pippenger and Golumbic) is the limit as $n\to\infty$ of the maximum, over $n$-vertex graphs $G$, of the number of induced copies of $H$ in $G$ divided by $\binom{n}{|H|}$; clearly $\mathrm{ind}(H)\le\mathrm{ind}(|H|,e(H))$. The random graph $G(n,p)$ with $p=\binom k2^{-1}$ gives $\mathrm{ind}(k,1)\ge1/e+o_k(1)$, and the complete bipartite graph with smaller part of size $n/k$ gives $\mathrm{ind}(k,k-1)\ge\mathrm{ind}(K_{1,k-1})\ge1/e+o_k(1)$; these constructions and additional data motivate the conjecture that $1/e$ is asymptotically tight. The $o_k(1)$ is necessary, as $\mathrm{ind}(3,1)=\mathrm{ind}(3,2)=3/4$. The authors prove that $\mathrm{ind}(k,\ell)<1-\varepsilon$ for an absolute $\varepsilon>0$ and all $0<\ell<\binom k2$, that $\mathrm{ind}(k,\ell)\le1/2+\varepsilon$ when $Ck\le\ell\le\binom k2-Ck$, that $\mathrm{ind}(k,\ell)=O(k^{-0.1})$ when $\min\{\ell,\binom k2-\ell\}=\Omega(k^2)$ (so the conjecture holds 'almost everywhere'), and that $\mathrm{ind}(k,\ell)\le3/4+o_k(1)$ for fixed $\ell$, with $1/2$ for $\ell=1$.

title: Conjecture 1.2 (The Large Inducibility Conjecture)
context_text: For a graph $G$ on $n$ vertices and $0\le\ell\le\binom k2$, let $I(n,k,\ell)$ be the maximum, over graphs $G$ on $n$ vertices, of the probability that a uniformly random $k$-subset of $V(G)$ spans exactly $\ell$ edges; this is non-increasing in $n$, and the edge-inducibility is $\mathrm{ind}(k,\ell)=\lim_{n\to\infty}I(n,k,\ell)$. It equals $1$ for $\ell\in\{0,\binom k2\}$ (empty or complete graphs) and satisfies $\mathrm{ind}(k,\ell)=\mathrm{ind}(k,\binom k2-\ell)$. For a graph $H$, the inducibility $\mathrm{ind}(H)$ (Pippenger and Golumbic) is the limit as $n\to\infty$ of the maximum, over $n$-vertex graphs $G$, of the number of induced copies of $H$ in $G$ divided by $\binom{n}{|H|}$; clearly $\mathrm{ind}(H)\le\mathrm{ind}(|H|,e(H))$. Here the $\limsup$ is that of the set of inducibilities of all graphs $H$ that are neither complete nor empty (its largest limit point). This is the analogue for graph inducibilities of the authors' Edge-statistics Conjecture (that for every $\varepsilon>0$, $\mathrm{ind}(k,\ell)\le1/e+\varepsilon$ for all large $k$ and $0<\ell<\binom k2$), which would imply it since $\mathrm{ind}(H)\le\mathrm{ind}(|H|,e(H))$. The value $1/e$ is attained asymptotically, e.g. $\mathrm{ind}(K_{1,k-1})=1/e+o_k(1)$, and $\mathrm{ind}(H)=\mathrm{ind}(k,1)\ge1/e+o_k(1)$ for the $k$-vertex graph with one edge. The authors prove that the inducibility of every graph that is neither complete nor empty is bounded away from $1$ by an absolute constant.
